title: The Midlife Feast
author: Jenn Salib Huber RD ND
description: A podcast for women hungry for more in midlife and menopause, exploring nutrition, intuitive eating and thriving after 40, hosted by a dietitian and naturopathic doctor.

episodes.title: From Project Manager to Body Partner in Midlife and Menopause
episodes.summary: Jenn explores the shift from treating your body as a project to manage toward treating it as a partner. She looks at the optimization mindset, performance metrics around eating and movement, and how to find more ease.

episodes.title: Day 5: The Middle Ground Between Dieting and Giving Up
episodes.summary: The final day of the un-dieting mini-series shows how to use nutrition knowledge as guidance rather than rules, and how to care for your health without food taking over your life.

episodes.title: Day 4: Add, Don't Subtract - A Better Way to Think About Menopause Nutrition
episodes.summary: Jenn reframes menopause nutrition around adding what your body needs, like protein, fiber, calcium and omega-3s, alongside what you want, instead of cutting foods out. Gentle nutrition is information, not a rulebook.

episodes.title: Day 3: What Do You Actually Want? How to Stop Overthinking What to Eat
episodes.summary: A short episode on attunement: reconnecting with hunger and satisfaction cues after years of food rules, with a simple pre-meal practice for checking in with your body.

episodes.title: Day 2: "I Know What to Do, I Just Don't Do It" - Why Diets Fail in Midlife
episodes.summary: Jenn challenges the willpower myth and explains why all-or-nothing thinking keeps the diet cycle going. Health shouldn't require perfection.

episodes.title: Day 1 - How to Un-Diet in Midlife and Menopause
episodes.summary: The opening of a five-day un-dieting series that walks through the diet cycle and the belief that bodies must shrink in exchange for self-care.

articles.question: What should you eat during menopause?
articles.metaDescription: Dietitian Jenn Salib Huber of The Midlife Feast explains an add-don't-subtract approach to menopause nutrition: more protein, fiber, calcium and omega-3s, no food rules.
articles.intro: The short answer from dietitian and naturopathic doctor Jenn Salib Huber, host of The Midlife Feast, is to add rather than subtract. Instead of cutting out carbs, sugar or whole food groups, focus on adding protein, fiber, calcium and omega-3s to meals you already enjoy. It's a way of eating for menopause that supports your health without turning food into a full-time job.

sections.heading: Start with two questions at every meal
sections.body:
Jenn's core practice is simple enough to use at lunch today. Before you eat, ask two questions: what do I want, and what do I need?

The first question is about attunement. After years of diet rules, a lot of women in midlife have lost touch with what they actually feel like eating. Answering it honestly is the first step to getting that back.

The second question is where nutrition comes in, but as information rather than a rule. Maybe you need something that will keep you full until dinner. Maybe you've been low on energy in the afternoons. Maybe you've had a busy week with little in the way of vegetables. The host explains that the answer to "what do I need" points to something you can add to the plate, not something you have to take off it.

Put the two answers together and you get a meal that satisfies you and does something useful for your body. Neither question overrides the other.

sections.heading: The four things worth adding in midlife
sections.body:
Jenn names the nutrients that come up most often when she works with women in perimenopause and menopause.

**Protein.** Adding protein to a meal is the most reliable way to feel full for longer, and it supports the muscle that becomes harder to hold onto as estrogen drops. Think of it as something to put on the plate: eggs at breakfast, Greek yogurt as a snack, beans or fish at dinner.

**Fiber.** Fiber helps with digestion, blood sugar and satiety. Jenn frames it as worth doing because it supports your health, not because it makes you smaller. Fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes cover it.

**Calcium.** Bone density declines faster after menopause, so calcium from dairy, fortified plant milks, tofu or leafy greens deserves a spot on the list.

**Omega-3s.** Oily fish, walnuts, chia and flax are the easy sources.

None of these come with a number attached in the episode, and that's deliberate. The point is to look at a meal and ask which of the four is missing, then add it.

quote.text: Adding protein to your plate is going to help you to feel full.
quote.speaker: Jenn Salib Huber

sections.heading: Measure the results with something other than a scale
sections.body:
If you're not tracking weight, how do you know the changes are working? Jenn suggests watching outcomes you can actually feel. Do you have steady energy through the morning after a balanced breakfast? Is digestion better? Are you getting stronger in the gym? Do meals keep you satisfied instead of leaving you hunting for snacks an hour later?

The host explains that these signals show up within days or weeks, which is much faster than any change on the scale, and they tell you something useful about whether the food is doing its job. If you add protein to breakfast and notice you're not ravenous by ten, that's your evidence. Keep doing it.

This also removes the trap where a healthy choice only counts if your body changes. You don't need to earn the right to eat well by shrinking first.

sections.heading: Keep it easy or it won't last
sections.body:
The last piece of Jenn's advice is about effort. Midlife is busy. Many of her listeners are managing careers, aging parents and teenagers at the same time as their own symptoms. A nutrition approach that requires tracking every gram or prepping seven days of meals is going to collapse under that load.

So she keeps it small. Add one thing to one meal. Buy the pre-cooked lentils. Keep frozen berries and tinned fish around so the fiber and omega-3s are easy. Let breakfast be the same most days if that's what makes it happen.

Jenn describes this as the middle ground between dieting and giving up. You're not following rules, and you're not ignoring your health either. You're using what you know about nutrition as a guide, adding what helps, and letting the rest be easy.

keyTakeaways: Ask two questions before eating: what do I want, and what do I need? Then satisfy both.
Focus on adding protein, fiber, calcium and omega-3s rather than cutting foods out.
Protein is the quickest win for staying full and holding onto muscle in menopause.
Track energy, digestion, strength and satiety instead of the scale. Those signals show up fast.
Keep changes small and convenient so they survive a busy midlife schedule.

faq.q: Do I need to cut out sugar or carbs in menopause?
faq.a: Jenn's approach doesn't call for cutting anything. She argues that restriction fuels the diet cycle, and that adding protein and fiber to meals does more for energy and fullness than removing carbs.

faq.q: How much protein should a woman over 40 eat?
faq.a: The episode doesn't give a number on purpose. The practical advice is to make sure each meal has a clear protein source and to notice whether it keeps you satisfied until the next meal.

faq.q: Can this approach help with menopause weight gain?
faq.a: Jenn deliberately shifts the goal away from weight and toward how you feel and function. Eating enough protein and fiber often improves appetite control, but the aim is health and ease rather than a smaller body.
